claim: In a 2008 Publishing Research Consortium survey of more than 3000 academics, 56% of respondents reported a preference for double-blind peer review.
source: In 2008 the Publishing Research Consortium conducted a survey in which more than 3000 academics were asked a series of questions about peer review. One of the clearest messages to emerge from the survey was a lack of support for single-blind peer review: 56% of respondents reported a preference for double-blind peer review, with just 25% preferring single-blind peer review, and only 13% preferring open peer review.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a survey conducted by the Publishing Research Consortium in 2008.

claim: In a 2008 Publishing Research Consortium survey of more than 3000 academics, 25% of respondents preferred single-blind peer review.

evidence: The claim is supported by data from a survey conducted by the Publishing Research Consortium in 2008.

claim: In a 2008 Publishing Research Consortium survey of more than 3000 academics, only 13% of respondents preferred open peer review.

claim: The most popular reason for preferring double-blind review was that it was seen as a more objective process, removing potential biases due to the author's institution, race, country, or personal biases.

evidence: The claim is supported by findings from the Publishing Research Consortium survey report.

claim: Taylor & Francis found a strong preference for double-blind review when it surveyed more than 7000 authors, reviewers and editors in 2015.

claim: About one-third of the manuscripts in the Springer Nature trial had to be excluded from gender analysis as the gender of the author could not be determined with sufficient confidence.

claim: Some reviewers, especially junior scientists, fear that critical but honest reviews of work by senior scientists would subject them to retribution by these senior figures.
source: "Some reviewers, especially junior scientists, fear that critical but honest reviews of work by senior scientists in the field would subject them to retribution by these senior figures, who might someday be asked to review their grants, papers, or promotions. Faced with such fears," Flier continues, "they might decline requests to do peer reviews, or provide less honest reviews seeking to pander to the authors. This isn't just a hypothetical concern – I have heard it from many faculty members at Harvard Medical School, as well as from some journal editors. To the extent it is real, this brings shame on a profession committed at its core to the pursuit of knowledge and truth."
evidence: The claim is supported by statements from Jeffrey Flier based on his experiences and conversations with faculty members and journal editors.
